title: Travis Kalanick's Atoms Raises $1.7 Billion to Build Industrial AI Empire
excerpt: The Uber co-founder's robotics company has secured major backing from Andreessen Horowitz and Uber, with plans to automate mining, food production, and heavy transport.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Atoms has raised $1.7 billion led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Uber as a backer.
  • The company focuses on automating food production, mining, and transport using AI and robotics.
  • Ben Horowitz will join Atoms' board as part of the investment deal.
  • Atoms acquired self-driving startup Pronto to enhance its autonomous technology capabilities.
  • The funding indicates a growing investor interest in physical AI applications.

From Ghost Kitchens to Industrial Automation

Atoms, the industrial robotics company founded by Uber co-founder and former CEO Travis Kalanick, has raised $1.7 billion in a funding round led by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. The deal includes both equity and debt financing, with Uber among the companies backing Kalanick's latest venture, according to the Economic Times.

https://x.com/digg/status/2080014958113558572

Ben Horowitz, co-founder of a16z, confirmed in a post on X that he will join Atoms' board as part of the investment. The funding marks a major endorsement for Kalanick's post-Uber ambitions, which have been quietly taking shape over the past eight years.

Atoms emerged publicly in March 2026 when Kalanick rebranded and expanded City Storage Systems, a holding company he founded in 2016 that previously housed CloudKitchens, his ghost kitchen business once valued at $15 billion. City Storage Systems had already raised more than $1 billion in equity and debt before the Atoms rebrand.

"Industrial AI is what will power the next industrial revolution."

— Atoms, in its funding announcement

Three Divisions, One Bet on Physical AI

The new capital will support Atoms' efforts to develop physical automation systems across large industrial sectors. The company is organized around three divisions: Atoms Food, which builds infrastructure for automated food production; Atoms Mining, focused on increasing productivity in mines; and Atoms Transport, which Kalanick has described as a "wheelbase for robots."

Atoms Food grew out of CloudKitchens and its Lab37 unit, which has deployed a kitchen robot called the Bowl Builder — a 19-foot-long, NSF-certified machine capable of producing 300 custom bowls per hour. Kalanick has said the system can cut restaurant labor costs from 30-35% of revenue to just 7-10%, a reduction of roughly 60%.

On the mining side, Atoms has developed retrofit kits that attach to existing machinery to make them autonomous. The company is running pilot programs with several large mining companies, according to Kalanick's comments to The Times. He has said autonomous mining technology could extract more lithium, gold, and other minerals with greater efficiency and safety.

"If you make technology that automates a mine, then you're able to get more lithium, you're able to get more gold. Name your mineral, you're going to be able to produce more with less."

— Travis Kalanick

Pronto Acquisition Adds Self-Driving Capability

Atoms has bolstered its autonomous technology through the acquisition of Pronto, the self-driving startup founded by Anthony Levandowski, a former Uber engineer who worked on the ride-hailing company's autonomous driving program. Pronto developed autonomous driving systems for haul trucks used in mining and construction — large, multimillion-dollar vehicles used for material transport.

Kalanick was already Pronto's largest investor before the full acquisition, according to TechCrunch. The deal adds autonomous vehicle capabilities to Atoms' broader portfolio as it works to automate industries that depend on heavy physical operations.

Atoms' Division Focus
›Atoms Food: Automates food production with robots.
›Atoms Mining: Enhances mining efficiency and safety.
›Atoms Transport: Develops autonomous vehicles for heavy transport.
›Bowl Builder: Produces 300 custom bowls/hour, reducing labor costs by 60%.

The company's transport division is also collecting hundreds of millions of miles of driving data to feed what Kalanick calls "physical AI models," according to The Times.

Kalanick's Specialized Robot Thesis

Kalanick has been explicit about his contrarian bet: task-specific industrial robots over general-purpose humanoids. While competitors like Boston Dynamics, Figure, and 1X chase bipedal machines, Atoms is building what Kalanick calls "gainfully employed robots" — machines optimized for high-cycle, harsh industrial environments.

"Humanoids have their place, but there's a lot of room for specialized robots that do things in an efficient, sort of industrial-scale kind of way, which is sort of where we play," Kalanick told TechCrunch in March.

The approach targets sectors where labor shortages are acute, safety regulations strict, and downtime expensive — conditions that make automation economically compelling without needing the flexibility of a general-purpose humanoid.

What Comes Next

Kalanick's Vision for Robotics
›Focus on specialized robots for industrial tasks.
›Contrasts with competitors pursuing humanoid robots.
›Targets sectors with labor shortages and strict safety regulations.
›Optimizes for efficiency in harsh industrial environments.

Atoms said the latest funding will support building more machines, increasing deployments, and tackling multiple industrial challenges simultaneously. The company is actively hiring engineers and builders to support its expansion, according to its LinkedIn announcement.

For the Indian diaspora, the deal underscores the continued dominance of Indian-origin entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley's biggest ventures. The $1.7 billion raise also signals growing investor appetite for physical AI — applying artificial intelligence to automate real-world operations rather than digital tasks — a sector likely to generate significant demand for engineering talent globally.
